data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are your community's envoy at a conference the forum convened. There is no organisation above the communities. The question before the conference: should the communities found an organisation to write a global analysis of the goals with proposals (a book of about 560 two-column pages) and to keep the infrastructure they share (a bench of analytical tools, a shelf of data), and on what charter? A charter fixes: coordination (a standing secretariat, an organisation that serves all; or a chair rotating among the members every twelve rounds), the rule by which the council admits a tool to the shared bench, who reviews sections at first (editor: the secretariat's or chair's editor alone; peers: two guild reviewers of other origins; panel: one reviewer from each member; forum: those the goals concern), and the rule for adopting the book. Your community's mission and order are given. Choose what to do among the options.

answer.title: The Distance to 2030: A Global Analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals from the World Development Indicators, with Proposals

chapters.title: Overview
chapters.question: How far has the world moved towards the Goals since 2015, and how far remains to 2030?

sections.title: The world stands short of most measurable targets
sections.question: What do the World Development Indicators show about progress from the 2015 base towards the 2030 targets, and where are the data too thin to judge?

chapters.title: Goal 1: Poverty
chapters.question: How much has poverty in all its forms fallen since 2015?

sections.title: Extreme poverty has fallen more slowly since 2015 than before
sections.question: What share of people lived below the international poverty line in 2015 and in the latest year, and does the trend reach zero by 2030?

sections.title: The depth of poverty tells a different story from its headcount
sections.question: How have the poverty gap and higher poverty lines moved since 2015?

sections.title: National poverty lines measure poverty by different yardsticks
sections.question: How far has poverty by national definitions fallen, and how comparable are the national series?

sections.title: Social protection covers a minority of the poorest
sections.question: What share of the poorest quintile is covered by social protection and labour programmes?

sections.title: Access to basic services remains unequal
sections.question: How do access to water, sanitation, electricity and accounts differ between poor and non-poor households?

sections.title: Disasters fall hardest on the poor
sections.question: How many people have been affected by disasters, and how well do the indicators capture exposure?

sections.title: Public spending on essential services varies widely
sections.question: What share of government spending goes to education, health and social protection?

chapters.title: Goal 2: Hunger and nutrition
chapters.question: How far has hunger fallen and nutrition improved since 2015?

sections.title: Undernourishment has risen since 2015
sections.question: What is the prevalence of undernourishment in 2015 and the latest year?

sections.title: Moderate and severe food insecurity affects a large share of the world
sections.question: What does the Food Insecurity Experience Scale show, and over which years?

sections.title: Stunting is falling but short of the 2025 and 2030 marks
sections.question: How have stunting and wasting among children under five changed, and will they meet the agreed targets?

sections.title: Overweight and anaemia form the other side of malnutrition
sections.question: How have child overweight and anaemia among women changed since 2015?

sections.title: Agricultural productivity has grown unevenly
sections.question: How have cereal yield and agricultural value added per worker changed, and can the doubling target be read from them?

sections.title: Pressure on agricultural land is rising
sections.question: How have agricultural land, fertiliser use and irrigation changed?

sections.title: Investment in agriculture lags its share of the economy
sections.question: What does the agriculture orientation index of government spending show?

chapters.title: Goal 3: Health and well-being
chapters.question: How far have deaths and disease fallen and health coverage expanded since 2015?

sections.title: Maternal mortality remains far above 70 per 100,000
sections.question: What is the maternal mortality ratio in 2015 and the latest year, and where is skilled attendance at birth lowest?

sections.title: Child and newborn deaths continue to fall
sections.question: How many countries already meet the thresholds of 25 under-five and 12 neonatal deaths per 1,000 live births?

sections.title: The epidemics of HIV, tuberculosis and malaria have receded but not ended
sections.question: How have the incidence of HIV, tuberculosis and malaria changed since 2015?

sections.title: Premature deaths from non-communicable disease fall slowly
sections.question: How has the probability of dying from the four main non-communicable diseases changed, and the suicide rate?

sections.title: Alcohol consumption has changed little
sections.question: What is total alcohol consumption per capita and its trend?

sections.title: Road traffic deaths missed the 2020 halving
sections.question: How has the road traffic mortality rate changed since 2015?

sections.title: Family planning needs are increasingly met
sections.question: How have demand satisfied by modern methods and the adolescent birth rate changed?

sections.title: Health coverage widens while out-of-pocket costs persist
sections.question: How have the service coverage index and catastrophic health spending changed?

sections.title: Pollution remains a leading cause of death
sections.question: What are mortality rates from air pollution, unsafe water and poisoning?

sections.title: Tobacco use declines
sections.question: How has the prevalence of tobacco use changed since 2015?

sections.title: Immunisation coverage fell and partly recovered
sections.question: How has coverage of DTP3 and measles vaccination changed since 2015?

sections.title: Health spending and the health workforce are thinnest where need is greatest
sections.question: How do health expenditure per capita and densities of physicians and nurses compare?

chapters.title: Goal 4: Education
chapters.question: How far have access to and completion of education improved since 2015?

sections.title: Completion rises while learning stalls
sections.question: How have primary and lower secondary completion rates and learning poverty changed?

sections.title: Out-of-school numbers have barely moved
sections.question: How many children and adolescents of school age are out of school?

sections.title: Pre-primary participation expands
sections.question: How has participation one year before primary entry changed?

sections.title: Tertiary enrolment grows unequally
sections.question: How has gross enrolment in tertiary education changed by sex and region?

sections.title: Gender parity is reached in enrolment in many countries but not all
sections.question: What do the gender parity indices for each level show?

sections.title: Youth literacy approaches universality in most regions
sections.question: How have youth and adult literacy rates changed, and how recent are the data?

sections.title: Trained teachers are scarce where pupils are many
sections.question: How have the share of trained teachers and pupil–teacher ratios changed?

sections.title: Public spending on education falls short of the benchmarks
sections.question: What share of GDP and of public spending goes to education?

chapters.title: Goal 5: Gender equality
chapters.question: How far have women's rights, safety and participation advanced since 2015?

sections.title: Legal equality advances unevenly
sections.question: How has the Women, Business and the Law index changed since 2015?

sections.title: Violence by intimate partners is poorly measured over time
sections.question: What share of women report violence by a partner, and how comparable are the surveys?

sections.title: Child marriage declines too slowly to end by 2030
sections.question: How has the share of women first married by 18 changed, and what is known of female genital mutilation?

sections.title: Unpaid care work is counted in few countries
sections.question: What do time-use data show about unpaid domestic and care work by sex?

sections.title: Women hold a minority of seats and senior posts
sections.question: How have women's shares of parliamentary seats and management positions changed?

sections.title: Many women do not decide on their own reproductive health
sections.question: What share of women make their own decisions on sexual relations, contraception and health care?

sections.title: Women's ownership of accounts and assets lags men's
sections.question: How large are gender gaps in account ownership and land ownership?

chapters.title: Goal 6: Water and sanitation
chapters.question: How far has access to water and sanitation improved and water stress eased since 2015?

sections.title: Safely managed drinking water remains out of reach for billions
sections.question: What share of people use safely managed and basic drinking water services?

sections.title: Sanitation lags water, and open defecation persists
sections.question: How have safely managed sanitation, basic hygiene and open defecation changed?

sections.title: Water stress is severe in several regions
sections.question: How have freshwater withdrawals as a share of internal resources changed?

sections.title: Water productivity rises slowly
sections.question: How much GDP is produced per cubic metre of water withdrawn?

chapters.title: Goal 7: Energy
chapters.question: How far have access to energy, renewables and efficiency advanced since 2015?

sections.title: Access to electricity nears universality outside sub-Saharan Africa
sections.question: What share of people had electricity in 2015 and the latest year, and who remains without it?

sections.title: Clean cooking advances slowly
sections.question: What share of people rely primarily on clean fuels and technologies for cooking?

sections.title: The renewable share of energy has risen little
sections.question: How has renewable energy's share of final energy consumption changed?

sections.title: Energy intensity improves at less than the doubled rate
sections.question: What has been the annual rate of improvement in primary energy intensity against the target rate?

chapters.title: Goal 8: Growth and decent work

carried.note: The call: To write a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, as a book of about 560 two-column pages (some 470 of prose and the rest a statistical annex and an account of how the book was made), from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, with base year 2015 and target year 2030; every number traceable to its data, every analysis replicated, every section reviewed.
commons/editor drafted the outline: The Distance to 2030: A Global Analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals from the World Development Indicators, with Proposals
The zero draft of the outline is before the council: 30 chapters, 156 sections

data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are your community's envoy in the partnership's council. The editor's zero draft of the book's outline is before the council. Propose at most four amendments that your community's mission and the book's quality call for (add a section or chapter, drop a section, change a section's question, more pages for a chapter), each with a reason, and list the chapters your community approves for the page budget (the pages are allotted by the Method of Equal Shares over the members' approvals: chapters few approve may be cut to two pages a section).

amendments.question: How many measurable targets is the world on course to meet by 2030, and by what count, what year and what reading of each target is that judged
amendments.why: The overview's headline claim must state its count, its year and its reading of the targets. Without these, the claim cannot be replicated by the guild or adopted by the cooperative.

amendments.title: Replication changes some findings
amendments.question: Which of the book's findings change when the analysis is rerun with other coverage, base years or aggregation weights
amendments.why: The cooperative drafts only from replicated analyses. Readers should see where a finding proved fragile on replication, which is the book's own evidence of quality.
By its own heading, waste and chemicals lie largely outside the indicators. The data gap belongs in chapter c29, not in two pages with no number to state.

amendments.title: North America's progress on the environmental Goals is measured thinly
amendments.question: Which environmental and consumption targets can be measured for North America from the World Development Indicators, and which cannot
amendments.why: The regional chapters should report coverage honestly. A high-income region's gaps in environmental measurement deserve the same scrutiny as those of poorer regions.

answer.note: The cooperative supports an outline built on declarative findings that each state a number, a year and a unit. It asks that every section be drafted only from analyses the guild has replicated. Where a replication fails, the section should say so rather than be cut silently.

amendments.title: Each section's series are chosen by one gatherer and checked by another
amendments.question: Which World Development Indicators series underpin each section, who chose and who checked them, and where did the checker disagree with the gatherer?
amendments.why: The commons keeps the shelf of data. A section recording the provenance of the series and the outcome of cross-origin checking lets readers judge every number and makes the book's method auditable.

amendments.question: For how many measurable targets do the World Development Indicators show the world short of the 2030 mark, at the latest year available, and for how many are data too sparse or the target too ambiguous to tell?
amendments.why: The headline should state its count, year and unit, and say openly where missing data or competing readings of a target prevent a verdict, as house style requires.
Financial soundness indicators lie largely outside the World Development Indicators, so the commons cannot shelve checked series for them. The pages serve the book better elsewhere.
These pages accommodate the added provenance section. The data-gaps chapter is where the book is honest about what its numbers can and cannot show.

answer.note: The commons approves the chapters whose series are well covered in the World Development Indicators and the chapters on data gaps and proposals. Where coverage is thin, as for oceans, waste and unpaid care, the shelf can support only short sections, and the text should say so.

amendments.title: Every finding in this book was replicated on the shared bench
amendments.question: How were the book's numbers produced and checked: which analyses were replicated by an analyst of another origin, where replications diverged, and how divergences were resolved?
amendments.why: The guild's method requires that every analysis be run on the shared bench and replicated before use; the reader needs a statement of that procedure and its outcomes to judge each finding's reliability.

amendments.question: How many measurable targets can be assessed from the World Development Indicators, and, for each, by how much does the latest value (with year and unit) fall short of or meet the 2030 mark under each stated reading of the target?
amendments.why: The heading 'stands short of most' asserts a count without defining the denominator or the reading of ambiguous targets; the question should oblige a replicable tally.

amendments.question: In how many countries with two comparable surveys did the income growth of the bottom 40 per cent exceed the mean, over which periods, and how sensitive is the count to survey comparability?
amendments.why: Shared-prosperity estimates depend heavily on which survey pairs are admitted; the section must state its coverage and test the result's robustness so another analyst can replicate it.

Medium and high-tech industry shares are sparsely reported in the World Development Indicators; two pages cannot support a replicable global finding, and the pages are better spent on the replication record.

answer.note: The guild asks the editor to require that every number cited carry its indicator code, year and unit, so that replication on the bench is possible. Where a target admits two readings, both should be computed and reported. The guild approves the chapters where indicator coverage is strongest and the methods chapters that make the book verifiable.

amendments.title: Who is left behind
amendments.question: Which groups, by sex, age, residence, income and disability, stand furthest from the targets, and how far do the World Development Indicators allow them to be seen at all?
amendments.why: The pledge to leave no one behind lacks a chapter of its own. The forum's mission is to say to whom the goals matter, and disaggregated gaps are now scattered across chapters or missing entirely. Where breakdowns by disability or rural residence are absent from the data, the chapter must say so.

amendments.title: Disability is almost absent from the indicators
amendments.question: What can the available data show about persons with disabilities against Goals 4, 8, 10 and 11, and where is that evidence absent?
amendments.why: Persons with disabilities are named in several targets yet appear nowhere in the draft. Their absence from the data should be recorded rather than passed over in silence.

amendments.question: Who bears the cost when financial systems are unsound, and which countries report the indicators that would reveal it?
amendments.why: As drafted, the section is technical and speaks to no one the goals concern. Tying it to the people exposed to financial crises keeps the chapter on inequality between people.

amendments.title: The shortfalls fall on identifiable people
amendments.question: How many people, in numbers rather than shares, remain in extreme poverty, hunger, without water and without schooling in the latest year available, and where do they live?
amendments.why: The overview speaks only in shares of targets. Stating counts of people, each with its year, keeps the book's opening in the service of those the goals concern.

data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are your community's envoy in the partnership's council. Read what the record shows of the book's making and choose among the options: you may propose to change who reviews sections (a compact of evaluation), how a section's adoption is decided (the rule and unit of count of the decision 'adopt section'), carry to the council a petition of your community's agents for a tool the bench lacks, vote on open proposals, say a note, or rest. Propose a change only when the record gives a reason; every change costs rounds.

The absence of persons with disabilities from the data should be recorded, not passed over.
Asking who bears the cost of unsound finance keeps the section on the people the goals concern.
Counts of people, each with its year, ground the overview in those the goals concern.
Three provenance sections in c29 duplicate one another; the guild's replication section covers the method more directly.
It demands count, year and unit and is open about missing data and ambiguous targets, as house style requires.
Forum proposes reframing c11 section 4 around the people exposed to financial crises, which is better than dropping it.
The added pages depend on a provenance section that duplicates the guild's.
Commons' wording also requires the gaps to be stated; prefer that version.
Readers deserve to know which findings proved fragile on replication.
Waste and chemicals affect communities directly, so the data gap should be stated where readers look for it.

data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are a gatherer lent to the commons of data. For the section below choose the series of the World Development Indicators that best answer its question: one to five, each with a reason of at most 25 words (what it measures, why it fits the targets, its known limits). Prefer series that measure a target's own indicator; prefer wide coverage. Choose only codes from the candidates. A petition is of one of two kinds: a tool, a computation over series the shelf holds that no tool of the bench makes (built by the guild if the council admits it); or data, a series the World Bank's catalogue does not hold (recorded as a gap of the shelf, which no tool can fill). Petition only when the section truly needs it.

series.why: Legal Framework Index (0-100) scores laws on women's economic opportunity, matching target 5.1's legal-equality focus; coverage is wide, but it records laws on the books, not practice.
Enforcement Perceptions Index (0-100) shows whether legal rights are applied in practice; it rests on expert perception and covers a shorter period.
Supportive Framework Index (0-100) measures the institutions and services that support the use of legal rights; it is a newer measure with a shorter history.

answer.note: The three WBL indices answer the question directly. The Legal Framework Index has the longest record; the enforcement and supportive indices may start later, so change since 2015 may not be comparable across all three.

series.why: Modelled stunting prevalence under five: the target's own indicator, with wide coverage and a continuous annual series for trend and 2025 and 2030 projection; modelled values carry uncertainty.
Wasting prevalence under five: the target's own indicator for wasting. Based on survey years, so coverage is uneven and series are not annual.
Modelled overweight prevalence under five: the third malnutrition indicator in target 2.2, with the 2025 and 2030 overweight targets; modelled, with wide uncertainty.
Severe wasting prevalence: shows the most acute malnutrition within wasting, though survey-based, with sparse coverage and irregular years.

answer.note: Modelled stunting is preferred over survey-only stunting (SH.STA.STNT.ZS) for coverage and trend. Targets can be read as global (2025: 40% fewer stunted children against 2012; 2030: wasting below 3%) or as national, so the reading must be stated. The shelf holds no projection tool for the target path.

series.why: Gross tertiary enrolment, total (% gross); the core measure of access under target 4.3, with wide coverage. Gross ratios can exceed 100 and ignore quality.
Female gross tertiary enrolment (% gross); allows regional aggregation and comparison by sex. Coverage is thinner in some low-income and conflict-affected countries.
Male gross tertiary enrolment (% gross); paired with the female series to show the direction and size of the gap over time.
Gender parity index for gross tertiary enrolment (female to male); summarises inequality in one figure. Values above 1 mean women are ahead; it hides differences in field of study.

answer.note: Gross enrolment counts all enrolled students regardless of age, so ratios can exceed 100 and are not comparable with net rates. Target 4.3 names affordability, technical and vocational education, and quality, which these series do not capture. Regional values depend on aggregate availability.

series.why: Primary completion rate, total: the target's own completion measure; wide coverage over decades. Limits: gross-type ratio can exceed 100% and ignores learning.
Lower secondary completion rate, total: tracks completion of the basic cycle named in target 4.1. Coverage thinner than primary, especially in earlier years.
Learning poverty: share of children at end-of-primary age below minimum reading proficiency, adjusted for out-of-school children. Few observation years; trend comparison limited.
Share of pupils below minimum reading proficiency at end of primary, low GAML threshold. Separates learning failure from school exclusion; sparse and irregular years.
Primary completion rate, female: with the male series (not selected) shows the gender gap in completion. Same limits as total.

answer.note: Completion series are administrative and cover many years; learning poverty rests on few assessment rounds, so a long learning trend cannot be drawn for many countries. Threshold choice affects the reading proficiency figures.

series.why: Gross primary enrolment gender parity index; target 4.5's own parity measure for the first level. Gross ratios can exceed 100 and mask over-age pupils.
Gross secondary enrolment parity index; shows whether parity holds at the level where girls' dropout or boys' disadvantage often emerges. Coverage thinner for some countries.
Gross tertiary enrolment parity index; many countries show values above 1, so disparity can run against men. Sparse in some low-income countries.
Combined primary and secondary parity index; wide coverage as a cross-check, though it blends two levels and hides differences between them.
Youth literacy parity index (ages 15-24); an outcome measure complementing enrolment. Survey-based, with infrequent observations and gaps in many countries.

answer.note: Preprimary parity is not among the candidates, so the levels covered are primary, secondary and tertiary. Gross enrolment parity does not capture disability, indigenous status or other vulnerability named in target 4.5.

Anaemia among women aged 15-49 (%) is the target's own indicator for women's nutrition; modelled estimates, with sparse survey data in many countries.
Anaemia among non-pregnant women aged 15-49 (%) separates the general trend from pregnancy; modelled, so subject to the same data limits.
Anaemia among pregnant women (%) addresses the target's mention of pregnant women; modelled, and series may end before recent years.
Anaemia among children aged 6-59 months (%) shows the wider burden alongside women's anaemia; modelled, not a target indicator.

answer.note: Modelled overweight series are preferred over survey-based ones for continuous coverage since 2015. The target sets no numeric goal for anaemia or overweight, so progress can be read in more than one way.

series.why: Cereal yield in kg per hectare is a direct, widely covered measure of land productivity; it omits non-cereal crops, livestock and the incomes of small-scale producers.
Cereal production in tonnes shows whether yield gains come from output growth, read together with area; it is a volume, not a productivity measure.
Land under cereal production separates yield gains from area expansion, so that growth in output can be attributed correctly.
Food production index (2014-2016 = 100) covers all food output beyond cereals; it is an aggregate volume, not per worker or per farm, and is not disaggregated by farm size.
Irrigated share of agricultural land helps explain uneven yield growth between countries; it is a context measure, not a target indicator.

answer.note: Target 2.3 is measured by agricultural value added per worker (indicator 2.3.1) and incomes of small-scale producers (2.3.2); neither appears among the candidates, and the candidate list contains no agricultural value added per worker series. Cereal yield and production indices can only indicate land productivity trends. The doubling target cannot be read from them, and no WDI series disaggregates by farm size, sex or indigenous status.

petition.name: Agricultural value added per worker (constant 2015 US$) and small-scale producer income
petition.need: Indicators 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 are needed to test the doubling target; the candidate shelf offers neither, and small-scale producer income is not held in the World Bank catalogue.

series.why: Target 5.2's own indicator: past-12-month partner violence among ever-partnered women aged 15-49. Survey-based, sparse over time, definitions and recall vary by survey.
Women's acceptance of wife-beating for any of five reasons; a norms proxy, not a measure of violence, drawn from household surveys with uneven years.
Prevalence of female genital mutilation, a harmful practice within the target's scope; covers only countries where it is concentrated and surveyed irregularly.
Women first married by age 18 (ages 20-24); a related harm to girls, though not partner violence, and survey-dependent.

answer.note: Only one series measures partner violence directly, and it rests on irregular surveys with differing questions, so trends cannot be read reliably. Attitude series are proxies.

series.why: Current health expenditure per capita in US$ gives the headline financing comparison for target 3.c; exchange-rate conversion understates purchasing power in poor countries.
Per-capita health spending in PPP dollars adjusts for price differences, making the gap between income groups more comparable; modelled estimates in low-income countries.
Nurses and midwives per 1,000 people measures the largest part of the health workforce; reporting years vary and definitions differ.
Domestic government health spending per capita shows public financing available, separating it from private and external sources; coverage thins in fragile states.
External health spending per capita shows dependence on aid in least developed countries and small island states; it is a flow, not a measure of adequacy.

answer.note: Physician density (SH.MED.PHYS.ZS) is not among the candidates, so physicians cannot be compared directly; community health workers (SH.MED.CMHW.P3) have sparse coverage and were left out. Workforce series are sparse in many countries.

series.why: Counts new displacements caused by disasters, the closest candidate to people affected; it covers displacement only, not injury or loss, and reporting varies by country.
Share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures; averaged 1990-2009, so it is dated, with no trend and uneven reporting.
Scores progress on national disaster risk reduction strategies (target 1.5 policy side); it measures preparedness, not exposure, and relies on self-reporting.
Rural population share is a rough proxy for exposure of livelihoods to climate shocks; it does not measure hazard or poverty directly.

answer.note: No candidate measures people affected by disasters annually, nor exposure by income group. Disaster displacement and the 1990-2009 average cover only part of the question; direct indicators of target 1.5 (affected persons, economic loss) are absent.

petition.name: People affected by disasters, by country and year
petition.need: Annual number of people affected, injured or left homeless by disasters per 100,000 population (the Sendai indicator for target 1.5.1), with disaster-related economic loss as a share of GDP.

series.why: Cereal yield in kg per hectare is a direct, widely covered measure of land productivity; it omits non-cereal crops, livestock and the incomes of small-scale producers.
Cereal production in tonnes shows whether yield gains come from output growth, read together with area; it is a volume, not a productivity measure.
Land under cereal production separates yield gains from area expansion, so that growth in output can be attributed correctly.
Food production index (2014-2016 = 100) covers all food output beyond cereals; it is an aggregate volume, not per worker or per farm, and is not disaggregated by farm size.
Irrigated share of agricultural land helps explain uneven yield growth between countries; it is a context measure, not a target indicator.

carried.note: Target 2.3 is measured by agricultural value added per worker (indicator 2.3.1) and incomes of small-scale producers (2.3.2); neither appears among the candidates, and the candidate list contains no agricultural value added per worker series. Cereal yield and production indices can only indicate lan

petition.name: Agricultural value added per worker (constant 2015 US$) and small-scale producer income
petition.need: Indicators 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 are needed to test the doubling target; the candidate shelf offers neither, and small-scale producer income is not held in the World Bank catalogue.

series.why: Modelled child overweight (under 5, %) gives a complete annual series from 2015, covering the target 2.2 indicator; estimates carry uncertainty in countries lacking surveys.
Anaemia among women aged 15-49 (%) is the target's own indicator for women's nutrition; modelled estimates, with sparse survey data in many countries.
Anaemia among non-pregnant women aged 15-49 (%) separates the general trend from pregnancy; modelled, so subject to the same data limits.
Anaemia among pregnant women (%) addresses the target's mention of pregnant women; modelled, and series may end before recent years.
Anaemia among children aged 6-59 months (%) shows the wider burden alongside women's anaemia; modelled, not a target indicator.

carried.note: Modelled overweight series are preferred over survey-based ones for continuous coverage since 2015. The target sets no numeric goal for anaemia or overweight, so progress can be read in more than one way.

series.why: Legal Framework Index (0-100) scores laws on women's economic opportunity, matching target 5.1's legal-equality focus; coverage is wide, but it records laws on the books, not practice.
Enforcement Perceptions Index (0-100) shows whether legal rights are applied in practice; it rests on expert perception and covers a shorter period.
Supportive Framework Index (0-100) measures the institutions and services that support the use of legal rights; it is a newer measure with a shorter history.

carried.note: The three WBL indices answer the question directly. The Legal Framework Index has the longest record; the enforcement and supportive indices may start later, so change since 2015 may not be comparable across all three.

series.why: Gross primary enrolment gender parity index; target 4.5's own parity measure for the first level. Gross ratios can exceed 100 and mask over-age pupils.
Gross secondary enrolment parity index; shows whether parity holds at the level where girls' dropout or boys' disadvantage often emerges. Coverage thinner for some countries.
Gross tertiary enrolment parity index; many countries show values above 1, so disparity can run against men. Sparse in some low-income countries.
Combined primary and secondary parity index; wide coverage as a cross-check, though it blends two levels and hides differences between them.
Youth literacy parity index (ages 15-24); an outcome measure complementing enrolment. Survey-based, with infrequent observations and gaps in many countries.

carried.note: Preprimary parity is not among the candidates, so the levels covered are primary, secondary and tertiary. Gross enrolment parity does not capture disability, indigenous status or other vulnerability named in target 4.5.

series.why: Primary completion rate, total: the target's own completion measure; wide coverage over decades. Limits: gross-type ratio can exceed 100% and ignores learning.
Lower secondary completion rate, total: tracks completion of the basic cycle named in target 4.1. Coverage thinner than primary, especially in earlier years.
Learning poverty: share of children at end-of-primary age below minimum reading proficiency, adjusted for out-of-school children. Few observation years; trend comparison limited.
Share of pupils below minimum reading proficiency at end of primary, low GAML threshold. Separates learning failure from school exclusion; sparse and irregular years.
Primary completion rate, female: with the male series (not selected) shows the gender gap in completion. Same limits as total.

carried.note: Completion series are administrative and cover many years; learning poverty rests on few assessment rounds, so a long learning trend cannot be drawn for many countries. Threshold choice affects the reading proficiency figures.

series.why: Gross tertiary enrolment, total (% gross); the core measure of access under target 4.3, with wide coverage. Gross ratios can exceed 100 and ignore quality.
Female gross tertiary enrolment (% gross); allows regional aggregation and comparison by sex. Coverage is thinner in some low-income and conflict-affected countries.
Male gross tertiary enrolment (% gross); paired with the female series to show the direction and size of the gap over time.
Gender parity index for gross tertiary enrolment (female to male); summarises inequality in one figure. Values above 1 mean women are ahead; it hides differences in field of study.

carried.note: Gross enrolment counts all enrolled students regardless of age, so ratios can exceed 100 and are not comparable with net rates. Target 4.3 names affordability, technical and vocational education, and quality, which these series do not capture. Regional values depend on aggregate availability.

series.why: Modelled stunting prevalence under five: the target's own indicator, with wide coverage and a continuous annual series for trend and 2025 and 2030 projection; modelled values carry uncertainty.
Wasting prevalence under five: the target's own indicator for wasting. Based on survey years, so coverage is uneven and series are not annual.
Modelled overweight prevalence under five: the third malnutrition indicator in target 2.2, with the 2025 and 2030 overweight targets; modelled, with wide uncertainty.
Severe wasting prevalence: shows the most acute malnutrition within wasting, though survey-based, with sparse coverage and irregular years.

carried.note: Modelled stunting is preferred over survey-only stunting (SH.STA.STNT.ZS) for coverage and trend. Targets can be read as global (2025: 40% fewer stunted children against 2012; 2030: wasting below 3%) or as national, so the reading must be stated. The shelf holds no projection tool for the target pat

series.why: Target 5.2's own indicator: past-12-month partner violence among ever-partnered women aged 15-49. Survey-based, sparse over time, definitions and recall vary by survey.
Women's acceptance of wife-beating for any of five reasons; a norms proxy, not a measure of violence, drawn from household surveys with uneven years.
Prevalence of female genital mutilation, a harmful practice within the target's scope; covers only countries where it is concentrated and surveyed irregularly.
Women first married by age 18 (ages 20-24); a related harm to girls, though not partner violence, and survey-dependent.

carried.note: Only one series measures partner violence directly, and it rests on irregular surveys with differing questions, so trends cannot be read reliably. Attitude series are proxies.

petition.name: Comparable repeated national survey series on partner violence, including lifetime prevalence, psychological violence and non-partner sexual violence
petition.need: The catalogue holds only past-12-month physical or sexual partner violence for ever-partnered women aged 15-49, with few repeat observations. No series covers lifetime prevalence, other forms of violence, trafficking, or women outside that age range.

series.why: Current health expenditure per capita in US$ gives the headline financing comparison for target 3.c; exchange-rate conversion understates purchasing power in poor countries.
Per-capita health spending in PPP dollars adjusts for price differences, making the gap between income groups more comparable; modelled estimates in low-income countries.
Nurses and midwives per 1,000 people measures the largest part of the health workforce; reporting years vary and definitions differ.
Domestic government health spending per capita shows public financing available, separating it from private and external sources; coverage thins in fragile states.
External health spending per capita shows dependence on aid in least developed countries and small island states; it is a flow, not a measure of adequacy.

carried.note: Physician density (SH.MED.PHYS.ZS) is not among the candidates, so physicians cannot be compared directly; community health workers (SH.MED.CMHW.P3) have sparse coverage and were left out. Workforce series are sparse in many countries.

petition.name: Physicians per 1,000 people (SH.MED.PHYS.ZS)
petition.need: The question asks about physician density, but the candidate shelf holds no physician series; the section needs it to compare physicians with nurses.

Share of the poorest quintile reached by social safety nets, the direct measure of coverage of the poor. Limited to countries with household surveys.
Share of the poorest quintile covered by social insurance, such as pensions; shows how far contributory schemes reach the poor. Survey years differ by country.
Coverage of unemployment benefits and active labour market programmes in the poorest quintile; completes the three programme types. Coverage is thin and surveys are few.
Share of all benefits going to the poorest quintile; measures targeting, not coverage, so it qualifies the coverage figures.

answer.note: No single series gives the poorest quintile's coverage by all programmes combined; the quintile figures are split by programme type and cannot be summed, as beneficiaries overlap. Data are survey-based, with irregular years.

series.why: Share of primary teachers with minimum required training; the nearest measure of target 4.c's own indicator. Coverage is patchy and national definitions of 'trained' differ.
Share of secondary teachers trained to national standard; shows whether the supply of qualified teachers extends beyond primary. Sparse in many low-income countries; standards differ.
Share of preprimary teachers trained; covers the level where qualification is often weakest. Coverage is narrower than for primary and secondary.
Number of primary teachers; with pupil enrolment it yields the pupil–teacher ratio, though the ratio itself is not among the candidates.
Number of secondary teachers; the headcount denominator for pupil–teacher ratios and the growth of supply. Pupil numbers must come from another series.

answer.note: No pupil–teacher ratio series appears among the candidates, so the ratio cannot be read directly. Trained-teacher shares use national definitions and are not strictly comparable across countries; coverage is thin, especially in least developed countries.

series.why: Target 4.6's own youth indicator: literacy of ages 15-24, both sexes. Coverage is wide, but surveys are irregular and recent values are missing for many high-income countries.
Adult literacy (15 and above) addresses the 'substantial proportion of adults' clause. Data are census- or survey-based and sparse in recent years.
Gender parity index of youth literacy shows whether women and men are reaching literacy equally, as target 4.6 requires. Same survey timing limits apply.
Adult female literacy reveals the gap in adult literacy, which is larger than among youth. Compared with the male series, it shows the gender gap. Years of observation vary by country.
Youth female literacy shows progress for young women, where the remaining deficits are concentrated. Missing years limit trend comparison.

answer.note: Literacy is reported irregularly, so the latest observation year differs by country and must be stated. The target also names numeracy, for which the shelf holds no series.

series.why: Indicator 5.5.1(a): share of parliamentary seats held by women; annual, near-global coverage since 1990. Measures lower or single houses combined; says nothing of influence.
Indicator 5.5.2: women's share of senior and middle management; ILO-modelled, so coverage is thinner and begins later. Definitions of management differ between countries.

answer.note: Local government seats (indicator 5.5.1(b)) and women in top executive posts are not among the candidates. Parliamentary seats and management shares cover only part of 'all levels of decision-making'.

data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are a gatherer of another origin, checking another gatherer's choice of series for the section below. Keep or drop each series (a reason of at most 20 words each), and add at most two candidates it missed that the section needs.

verdicts.why: Core total gross tertiary enrolment measure for target 4.3, with broad coverage.
Female enrolment is needed for the by-sex comparison across regions and over time.
Male enrolment pairs with the female series to show the size of the gap.
Parity index summarises the sex gap in one figure and shows which sex leads.

add.why: Female tertiary attainment shows whether enrolment translates into completed qualifications, complementing access with outcomes.
Male attainment pairs with the female series to compare completion by sex.

series.why: Share of primary teachers with minimum required training; the nearest measure of target 4.c's own indicator. Coverage is patchy and national definitions of 'trained' differ.
Share of secondary teachers trained to national standard; shows whether the supply of qualified teachers extends beyond primary. Sparse in many low-income countries; standards differ.
Share of preprimary teachers trained; covers the level where qualification is often weakest. Coverage is narrower than for primary and secondary.
Number of primary teachers; with pupil enrolment it yields the pupil–teacher ratio, though the ratio itself is not among the candidates.
Number of secondary teachers; the headcount denominator for pupil–teacher ratios and the growth of supply. Pupil numbers must come from another series.

carried.note: No pupil–teacher ratio series appears among the candidates, so the ratio cannot be read directly. Trained-teacher shares use national definitions and are not strictly comparable across countries; coverage is thin, especially in least developed countries.

petition.name: pupil-teacher ratio from enrolment and teacher counts
petition.need: Computes pupil–teacher ratios by level from enrolment and teacher counts held on the shelf, by country, year and income group, for comparison with trained-teacher shares.

series.why: Coverage of all social protection and labour programmes, share of population; the whole-population benchmark for target 1.3. Survey-based, uneven years, sparse in high-income countries.
Share of the poorest quintile reached by social safety nets, the direct measure of coverage of the poor. Limited to countries with household surveys.
Share of the poorest quintile covered by social insurance, such as pensions; shows how far contributory schemes reach the poor. Survey years differ by country.
Coverage of unemployment benefits and active labour market programmes in the poorest quintile; completes the three programme types. Coverage is thin and surveys are few.
Share of all benefits going to the poorest quintile; measures targeting, not coverage, so it qualifies the coverage figures.

carried.note: No single series gives the poorest quintile's coverage by all programmes combined; the quintile figures are split by programme type and cannot be summed, as beneficiaries overlap. Data are survey-based, with irregular years.

verdicts.why: Target's own stunting indicator; annual modelled series suits trend and 2025/2030 projection.
Target's wasting indicator; needed to judge progress toward the wasting mark, despite uneven survey years.
Overweight is the third malnutrition measure in target 2.2; annual modelled series allows trend.
Not a target indicator; sparse, irregular survey data add little beyond the wasting series.

add.why: Undernourishment is the Goal 2 hunger context for the wider malnutrition picture and target 2.1.
Child anaemia reflects micronutrient deficiency, another form of malnutrition under target 2.2.

series.why: Target 4.6's own youth indicator: literacy of ages 15-24, both sexes. Coverage is wide, but surveys are irregular and recent values are missing for many high-income countries.
Adult literacy (15 and above) addresses the 'substantial proportion of adults' clause. Data are census- or survey-based and sparse in recent years.
Gender parity index of youth literacy shows whether women and men are reaching literacy equally, as target 4.6 requires. Same survey timing limits apply.
Adult female literacy reveals the gap in adult literacy, which is larger than among youth. Compared with the male series, it shows the gender gap. Years of observation vary by country.
Youth female literacy shows progress for young women, where the remaining deficits are concentrated. Missing years limit trend comparison.

carried.note: Literacy is reported irregularly, so the latest observation year differs by country and must be stated. The target also names numeracy, for which the shelf holds no series.

series.why: Indicator 2.1.1 itself: share of the population with insufficient habitual food intake. Wide coverage; modelled three-year averages and a lagged latest year limit precision.
Indicator 2.1.2: moderate or severe food insecurity from the FIES survey. Complements undernourishment by measuring access; coverage begins around 2015 and is modelled.
Severe food insecurity, the narrower tier of indicator 2.1.2, close to hunger. Shares the short time series and survey-based limits of the moderate-or-severe measure.

carried.note: Undernourishment is published as three-year averages, so 2015 and the latest year are smoothed values. Child stunting and wasting address target 2.2 and are left to that section.

verdicts.why: Core series for legal equality since 2015; matches target 5.1 and the section's question directly.
Perception-based with a short history, so it cannot show change since 2015; not a measure of legal change.
Measures supporting institutions, not laws, and has a short history; weak fit for change since 2015.

add.why: Violence against women shows whether legal protections coincide with outcomes; target 5.1 is tied to Safety, but data are sparse.

series.why: Target 3.6's own indicator: road traffic deaths per 100,000 population. Wide country coverage, but modelled estimates, published at intervals, with under-reporting in weak registration systems.
Share of all deaths caused by injury, of which road traffic is one part. Gives context only; it is not specific to roads and shifts with other causes.
Completeness of death registration with cause-of-death information shows where road death counts rest on records rather than models, qualifying the trend.

carried.note: Only SH.STA.TRAF.P5 measures the target directly. Injury injury-share and registration completeness are supporting context. Counts of injuries, which target 3.6 also names, are absent from the candidates.

series.why: Indicator 5.5.1(a): share of parliamentary seats held by women; annual, near-global coverage since 1990. Measures lower or single houses combined; says nothing of influence.
Indicator 5.5.2: women's share of senior and middle management; ILO-modelled, so coverage is thinner and begins later. Definitions of management differ between countries.

carried.note: Local government seats (indicator 5.5.1(b)) and women in top executive posts are not among the candidates. Parliamentary seats and management shares cover only part of 'all levels of decision-making'.

series.why: Target 1.2's own indicator: share of population below each country's national poverty line. Coverage is sparse and survey years differ; lines and methods vary across countries.
Captures poverty in all its dimensions (monetary, education, basic infrastructure), which target 1.2 names. Covers fewer countries and years, and the method differs from national definitions.

UNDP and OPHI multidimensional headcount offers a second dimensional reading of 'all its dimensions'. Indicator sets and thresholds differ from the World Bank measure; coverage is limited to developing countries.

Societal poverty line combines an absolute floor with a median-linked relative component, giving a common yardstick against which national lines can be compared. Uses a different definition from national lines.
Headcount at $4.20 a day (2021 PPP) offers a fixed international benchmark for comparing national series. It is not a national definition.

answer.note: National lines are set by each country, so levels are not comparable across countries; only trends within a country are reliable, and only where survey methods stay constant. Gaps in years and countries are large. International and multidimensional series serve as cross-checks, not substitutes.

series.why: Net official flows from FAO, current US$; a direct channel of agricultural support to developing countries. Covers one agency only and says nothing of domestic spending.
Net official flows from IFAD, current US$; IFAD finances rural and agricultural development. Recipient countries only, and flows vary sharply by year.
Total net ODA received, current US$; frames external finance available to developing countries for target 2.a. Not specific to agriculture.
Net ODA received as % of central government expense; shows reliance on aid relative to national budgets. Sector split is absent.
Net FDI inflows as % of GDP; comparable across many countries as a proxy for investment. Not specific to agriculture.

answer.note: The agriculture orientation index of government spending (SDG indicator 2.a.1) is not among the candidates. The series chosen are proxies for external finance and cannot show agriculture's share of government spending against its share of the economy.

series.why: Net official flows from FAO, current US$; a direct channel of agricultural support to developing countries. Covers one agency only and says nothing of domestic spending.
Net official flows from IFAD, current US$; IFAD finances rural and agricultural development. Recipient countries only, and flows vary sharply by year.
Total net ODA received, current US$; frames external finance available to developing countries for target 2.a. Not specific to agriculture.
Net ODA received as % of central government expense; shows reliance on aid relative to national budgets. Sector split is absent.
Net FDI inflows as % of GDP; comparable across many countries as a proxy for investment. Not specific to agriculture.

carried.note: Each country is counted against both thresholds in the latest common year. The target sets 'at least as low as' thresholds, so values equal to 25 and 12 count as met. A country must meet both.

Secondary gross enrolment parity index; needed for the secondary level.
Tertiary gross enrolment parity index; shows disparity running against men.

Youth literacy parity is an outcome complement to enrolment, though sparse and survey-based.

series.why: Target 1.2's own indicator: share of population below each country's national poverty line. Coverage is sparse and survey years differ; lines and methods vary across countries.
Captures poverty in all its dimensions (monetary, education, basic infrastructure), which target 1.2 names. Covers fewer countries and years, and the method differs from national definitions.

UNDP and OPHI multidimensional headcount offers a second dimensional reading of 'all its dimensions'. Indicator sets and thresholds differ from the World Bank measure; coverage is limited to developing countries.

Societal poverty line combines an absolute floor with a median-linked relative component, giving a common yardstick against which national lines can be compared. Uses a different definition from national lines.
Headcount at $4.20 a day (2021 PPP) offers a fixed international benchmark for comparing national series. It is not a national definition.

carried.note: National lines are set by each country, so levels are not comparable across countries; only trends within a country are reliable, and only where survey methods stay constant. Gaps in years and countries are large. International and multidimensional series serve as cross-checks, not substitutes.

data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are an analyst of the guild. Plan the analyses the section's writer will need for a substantive section: four to eight steps, each a tool of the bench with its parameters, using only the section's accepted series; analyse each main series for the regions and for the countries, and read the distribution, the convergence, the breaks and the links between series where they answer the question. Use trend with the target the targets' text states (give its reading in target_reading; null when the target names no number) and desired direction; levels for the regional picture; spread, convergence, breaks and links where they answer the question. A petition is of one of two kinds: a tool, a computation over series the shelf holds that no tool of the bench makes (built by the guild if the council admits it); or data, a series the World Bank's catalogue does not hold (recorded as a gap of the shelf, which no tool can fill). Petition only when the section truly needs it.

series.why: Modelled maternal mortality ratio per 100,000 live births; the indicator for target 3.1, with wide coverage, enabling 2015 and latest-year comparison. Modelled, so uncertainty ranges are wide.
Births attended by skilled health staff (% of total); the second indicator of target 3.1, used to locate lowest coverage. Survey years differ and many countries lack recent data.
Number of maternal deaths shows where the absolute burden falls, complementing the ratio. Modelled, and reported only at intervals.

answer.note: The target of 70 per 100,000 is a global ratio, so country values need a live-birth weighted aggregate. Skilled attendance is survey-based, with uneven years across countries.

series.why: Headcount below $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) is the current international extreme poverty line, the indicator for target 1.1; wide coverage, survey-based, gaps between survey years.
Poverty gap at $3.00 a day shows depth of extreme poverty, indicating how far those below the line are from it; survey-year gaps.
Headcount at $4.20 a day shows persistence just above the extreme line, where many people remain vulnerable; not a target indicator.
National poverty lines give a country-defined complement to the international line; definitions differ across countries, limiting comparison.

answer.note: The $1.25 line in the target text is superseded; the $3.00 line at 2021 PPP is used. Survey data are sparse and lagged, so the latest year varies by country and 2015 values may be interpolated.
